name: Lip plumper (capsaicin)
lead: A capsaicin lip plumper is a topical cosmetic applied to the lips that uses an irritant, most often capsaicin from chili peppers, sometimes with menthol, cinnamon, peppermint or ginger, to produce a brief tingling or warming sensation and a short-lived swelling that makes the lips look fuller and more defined.[1] It is used as a non-injectable, low-cost way to get fuller-looking lips for an evening, a photo or a makeup look, and is applied as a gloss, balm or serum before or under lipstick.[1]

Irritant formulas are described as working by stimulating nerve endings and increasing local blood flow, with effects reported to last from minutes to a few hours.[1][4] Capsaicin acts on the TRPV1 receptor on sensory nerves, the same channel that registers noxious heat, which is why the lips feel warm.[8][13] A separate class of hydration-based plumpers relies on humectants such as hyaluronic acid and does not aim to irritate; these give a smoother, subtler look and are the formulas that tend to be marketed as tingle-free.[1]

Published research consists of small, mostly open-label studies of proprietary products, many of which combine several ingredients. Case reports and reviews document contact urticaria and allergic contact reactions to lip cosmetics, including plumpers.[2][3][4] Lip plumpers sit at the low-cost, reversible end of a spectrum of lip-enhancement options that also includes injectable fillers, fat transfer and implants.[12]

paras: Irritant-based plumpers apply a mild irritant to the lips so that the skin reddens and swells slightly, which is perceived as added volume.[1] Users commonly describe a tingling, warming or stinging sensation that products present as a sign the formula is active, and the intensity ranges from barely noticeable to strong depending on concentration and the individual.[1]

Capsaicin acts on heat-sensitive receptors on sensory nerves, which is why it feels hot; the same activation is described as driving vasodilation and mild inflammation.[1] The receptor, TRPV1, was identified in 1997 by David Julius's group, who screened a library of sensory-neuron genes for clones that made cells respond to capsaicin; Julius shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work including this discovery.[13] TRPV1 opens in response to temperatures above about 43 degrees Celsius, acidity and capsaicin, which explains why a chili compound produces a sensation of heat without any actual temperature change.[13]

Hydration-based products use ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, glycerin and peptides and are described as giving a smoother, subtler effect through moisture and surface smoothing rather than irritation.[1] Some products combine both approaches, pairing a small amount of capsicum extract with humectants.[1]

Capsaicin was first extracted in impure form by Christian Friedrich Bucholz in 1816 and obtained in nearly pure form by J. C. Thresh in 1876; it is rated at about 16 million Scoville heat units and is classed as a skin irritant.[8] In clinical medicine it is used in 8% patches for neuropathic pain, an indication where trials such as a 369-patient phase 3 study in diabetic neuropathy compared the patch with placebo.[8][9] Lip plumpers use far lower concentrations of capsaicin or capsicum extract for a cosmetic sensation rather than a therapeutic one.[1]

Examples cited in cosmetics coverage include Grande Cosmetics GrandeLIPS (a tingle-free formula with hyaluronic acid, vitamin B3 and caffeine), Dior Addict Lip Maximizer, which combines capsicum frutescens with hyaluronic acid, and DuWop Lip Venom.[1]

Interest in fuller lips has a long surgical and injectable history. Around 1900 surgeons tried injecting paraffin into the lips, and liquid silicone was used from the early 1960s before being abandoned roughly thirty years later over health concerns.[12] Injectable bovine collagen became the benchmark around 1980, though it required an allergy test and gave short-lived results, and hyaluronic acid gels such as Restylane and Juvederm later became widely used, typically lasting around six months to a year or more.[12] Fat transfer, calcium hydroxylapatite and implant materials are other documented options, and the American Society of Plastic Surgeons reported 778,000 Restylane procedures in 2006.[12]

Within this landscape, Wikipedia lists lip plumpers containing irritants such as capsaicin, and suction pumps that draw blood into the lips, as the non-surgical alternatives that give temporary fullness without needles.[12] Overfilled results from injectables are commonly mocked as a 'trout pout', which is part of why some people look to a reversible product that fades the same day.[12]

Grokipedia credits DuWop Cosmetics' Lip Venom, launched in 1999, with introducing the first topical plumper, and describes the category growing through the 2000s before a shift toward tingle-free, hydration-based formulas and a renewed interest in the late 2010s.[1] This history comes from a single AI-generated source.

The same source says that by the mid-2000s about 21 percent of lip product users expressed interest in plumping effects, that early products relied mostly on irritants, and that later launches emphasised comfortable hydration and gradual, natural-looking volume amid a broader trend toward subtle, non-invasive beauty.[1]

The best-documented studies test branded products. A four-week open-label single-centre study of a two-step lip treatment (a renewal formula with growth factors, hyaluronic acid, marine filling spheres and a tripeptide, plus a plumper containing niacin) assessed moisturisation and fullness at baseline, week 2 and week 4; it tested a combined regimen rather than capsaicin alone.[5]

A 2018 single-site open-label trial in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology evaluated duration, efficacy and safety of a novel plumper,[6] and a 2017 study in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science asked how long the volumising effect of a ginger-based plumper lasts.[7] A 2009 case report discussing lip plumpers noted that they are designed to increase lip volume from minutes to days after application and described the sociocultural reasons for their use.[3] Grokipedia summarises the literature as showing short-lived volume in small unblinded studies.[1]

Users and brands describe the visible result as a glossier, rosier, more defined lip that is noticeable in photos for a short window. The swelling is generally described as modest compared with injectables, and the appearance returns to baseline as the sensation fades.[1][12]

A 2009 case report in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology described contact urticaria from a lip plumper in a young boy and discussed the mechanisms and the social reasons for use.[3] A 2016 review catalogued cosmetic ingredients that cause immediate-type contact reactions, diagnosed by prick testing or detection of specific IgE,[2] and a 2024 systematic review examined allergic contact dermatitis to lip-care products.[4]

Grokipedia reports that frequent use of irritant formulas may cause dryness, scaling, increased sensitivity or allergic reactions, and that experts suggest caution for people with sensitive lips.[1] Capsaicin itself is a recognised skin and eye irritant on contact, which is why removal of the substance is the usual response to over-exposure.[8] Hydration-based formulas are described as the lower-irritation option and are often preferred for sensitive skin or daily wear.[1]

The studies available are small and mostly open-label, and they commonly test proprietary multi-ingredient products rather than capsaicin alone.[5][6][7] The 2009 combination-treatment study followed participants for four weeks with clinical assessments at baseline, week 2 and week 4, and looked at moisturisation and fullness for a regimen that included a niacin-based plumper.[5] The 2018 trial and the 2017 ginger-based study examined how long volumising effects last after a single product is applied.[6][7]

Capsaicin has a much larger research base outside cosmetics: a phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled trial of the 8% patch in painful diabetic neuropathy (369 patients) reported a 27.4% versus 20.9% reduction in average daily pain, and reviews list topical capsaicin among treatments for neuropathic pain and burning mouth syndrome.[9] Those studies concern pain, not lip appearance. No large randomized trial of a capsaicin-only lip plumper was identified.

Grokipedia credits DuWop Cosmetics' Lip Venom (1999) with creating the category, and plumpers are now sold by many mainstream and indie beauty brands as glosses and treatments.[1] A T Nation forum poster in 2010 mentions that they had always loved Lip Venom and bought a plumper costing close to forty dollars, an example of the product appearing in general lifestyle conversation.[10]

In lifting-and-nutrition forums capsaicin appears mainly as a hot-sauce ingredient and as a topical for sore joints rather than as a lip product.[11] Within appearance communities, plumpers are discussed alongside fillers as one of the cheaper options for fuller lips, with injectables providing longer-lasting results.[12]

card.summary: A chili-based lip gloss that irritates the lips into swelling for a short while; the volume is brief and the evidence thin.
card.note: Irritant reactions and contact allergy to lip cosmetics are documented.

quick.overview:
Capsaicin lip plumpers are glosses or balms that contain a chili-derived irritant, sometimes alongside menthol, cinnamon or ginger. They produce a tingle or burn and a short-lived swelling that makes lips look fuller.

Products are positioned as a needle-free alternative to filler. Published evidence is limited to small, mostly open-label studies of branded products.
quick.mechanism: Capsaicin activates heat-sensitive receptors on sensory nerves and is described as increasing blood flow and causing mild swelling. The effect is reported to last from minutes to a few hours.
quick.risks: Case reports and reviews document contact urticaria and allergic contact reactions to lip cosmetics. Grokipedia reports that frequent use of irritant formulas may cause dryness and sensitivity.

chain: Capsaicin or another irritant is applied to the lips
Nerve endings are stimulated and local blood flow rises
Lips swell slightly and look fuller for minutes to hours
angle.text: The product is applied like a lip gloss and the lips look rosier and fuller as the tingling sets in. The look is described as temporary, fading as the sensation subsides.
